What Claude Skills Actually Are, and What They Aren't

What Claude Skills Actually Are, and What They Aren't

A practical map of the three layers people keep confusing, and the one rule that makes skills work.

Two patterns I see almost every day right now. One person is convinced that adding a skill called security will somehow make their agent safer. Another person has a 600 line skill that is, on inspection, a copy of their cursor rules with a different file extension. Both are confused in the same shape. They have heard that skills are powerful and they have decided to treat skills as a magic word.

Skills are not a magic word. They are a specific thing with a specific job, and the discipline that makes them useful is the discipline of knowing what belongs in one and what does not.

Hit reply and tell me what you have been putting in your skills folder. I want to see if the patterns I am seeing match yours.

Three things to hold onto:

  • A skill is procedural knowledge loaded just in time. It is not a security boundary, not the CLAUDE.md file, and not a subagent. Confusing those is most of the pain people are feeling right now.
  • The job of a skill is to make Claude reliably good at one repeatable task. Facts and conventions belong in CLAUDE.md. Procedures belong in skills. Work that needs fresh eyes belongs in a subagent.
  • Skills can run code. They are an attack surface, not a defense. Installing a skill from a stranger is closer to running a script than reading a doc.

The confusion under the confusion

The reason people are getting skills wrong is that the word "skill" sounds like a capability. People hear capability and assume the skill is what gives Claude the ability to do the thing. So they imagine skills as gates, as guardrails, as the place where you tell the agent what it is allowed to do.

That is the wrong mental model. A skill does not add capability. The model already has the capability. A skill adds a procedure for using the capability well in a specific situation. The skill is the recipe, not the kitchen.

Once you see it that way, the second wave of misuse becomes obvious. People keep writing skills that are not procedures at all. They are project conventions, naming rules, do-not-do lists, code style preferences. Those are facts. Facts belong in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, which load once at the start of a session and stay. A procedure belongs in a skill, which loads only when the procedure is needed and stays out of the way the rest of the time.

The difference matters because tokens matter. If every fact lived in a skill, the skill would never load when it should. If every procedure lived in CLAUDE.md, you would be carrying around a hundred procedures you do not need on any given turn.

What a skill actually is, on disk

A skill is a folder. Inside is at least one file called SKILL.md. The folder lives in one of a small number of places, and the place determines who can use it.

~/.claude/skills/my-skill/SKILL.md is a personal skill, available in every project on your machine. .claude/skills/my-skill/SKILL.md inside a project is a project skill, available only in that repo and shipped with it when you push. Plugin skills live inside a plugin and travel with the plugin.

The SKILL.md file has two parts. YAML frontmatter at the top, and markdown instructions below.

The name is what shows up in listings. The description decides whether your skill ever gets loaded, because it is the only thing Claude sees about your skill at the start of a session. Anthropic calls this progressive disclosure. The short version: the model loads the names and descriptions of every skill you have, which costs almost nothing, and loads the full body of a skill only when the description matches the work being asked for.

That is the whole trick. Skills are cheap to have and expensive to load, so they are designed to stay closed until needed. Vague description, the skill never opens. Specific description, the skill opens at the right moment.

The three layers people confuse

This is the part I want to make sticky, because it gets tangled almost every week.

There are three different things in the Claude Code ecosystem that all feel like "telling the model how to behave." They are not interchangeable.

CLAUDE.md (or AGENTS.md) is for facts. Project structure, naming conventions, preferences, the tech stack, what not to do. Things that should be true for every turn of every session in this repo. Loads at the start and stays. If you only have one file, this is the one to have.

Skills are for procedures. Multi-step tasks that you run again and again. Generating a particular kind of PDF. Publishing to a particular blog. Spinning up a particular type of test. Things that should be reliably the same every time, but do not need to be in context when you are doing something unrelated.

Subagents are for isolation. Work that should run in a clean context. Reviewing a diff without the bias of having just written it. Doing research that produces a small distilled answer and discards the rest. Running something in parallel with the main thread. Subagents get their own context window and return results.

A useful test. If I asked you the same thing in a brand new session tomorrow, which one would I want?

If the answer should be the same every time and is part of who the project is, CLAUDE.md. If the answer requires you to follow a specific procedure I have written down, skill. If the answer needs fresh eyes uncontaminated by what just happened, subagent.

I keep seeing cursor rules pasted into a SKILL.md and then nobody can figure out why the rules are not being followed. They are not being followed because the skill is not loading. The description does not match anything the user is asking for, because the rules are not a thing the user asks for, they are an ambient fact about the project. Put them in CLAUDE.md and they will work.

What skills are perfect for

The clearest signal that something should be a skill is that you keep copy-pasting the same instructions into the chat.

Last week I built a small component library for screenshots that I use across my book chapters and my Medium articles. Mac terminal windows, code editors, fake Claude Code UI, that kind of thing. I had the script. I had the working HTML file. But every time I wanted a new screenshot I was re-explaining the same thing. "Use the templates in build_screens.py, render scenes.html at viewport 1800x2000, screenshot the selector, here is the wrapper class for a sage backdrop."

That is a skill. Specifically a skill with a description that enumerates the actual things you do, so the model can match against them. The body lists the existing template ids, the render and screenshot workflow, the convention for backdrops. It is about a page. It loads only when I am asking for a mockup. The rest of the time it sits there costing nothing.

The other place skills earn their keep is publishing. I have skills for the Gloss blog, for my Substack newsletter, and one in progress for Amazon KDP. Each one is a procedure with real steps. Check the API key. Fetch the current post list. Apply the brand style for images. Save to the right folder. Push. The skill encodes the steps and the model follows them. Without the skill I would explain those steps again every Wednesday morning.

A short list, by way of pattern recognition. Things that work well as skills:

  • Publishing or deployment procedures with multiple steps and a specific style
  • Generating documents (PDF, slide deck, brief) with a particular layout
  • Running a particular kind of evaluation, benchmark, or check
  • Working with a specific external API where the call sequence matters
  • A workflow that involves both a script and a write-up of how to use it

If the thing is "follow this sequence of steps, in this order, with this style," it is probably a skill.

What skills are not

This is the part that needs to be loud, because the misconceptions here are the ones causing real harm.

A skill is not a security mechanism. I cannot say this strongly enough. A skill is a folder you tell the model to read. The model reads it. If the skill says "do not delete production data," the model will do its best to follow that instruction, the same way it would follow any other instruction. The skill does not enforce anything. It is not a permission system. It is not an allowlist or a denylist. The actual permission system is the harness, the tool settings, and the sandbox the agent runs in.

Worse, a skill is itself an attack surface. Skills can include scripts. Scripts can run. If you install a skill from someone you do not know, you are installing executable code on your machine and giving it to your agent to use. Anthropic's docs are explicit about this. "Skills provide Claude with new capabilities through instructions and code... malicious skills may introduce vulnerabilities or direct Claude to exfiltrate data." Read the SKILL.md. Read the scripts. Treat installing a skill like installing a CLI tool from npm. Sometimes you trust the source and you ship. Sometimes you read it first.

Putting a skill called safe-mode on top of an agent that has shell access does not make the agent safer. It makes it slightly more verbose when it does something dangerous.

A skill is not the CLAUDE.md file. This is the cursor rules confusion. Project conventions, style preferences, lists of things to never do, names of internal services, environment quirks. All of that is a fact about the project, not a procedure. It belongs in CLAUDE.md (or AGENTS.md, which is the cross-tool open standard for the same idea) and loads at the start of the session.

The tell that you have written a fact-skill is that the description is vague and Claude rarely loads it. You wrote "Coding conventions for this project." Nothing the user types matches that. So the skill sits unused and you wonder why the rules are being ignored.

A skill is not a subagent. When a skill runs, it runs in the main conversation with the main context. It does not get a clean window. It does not run in parallel. If you need fresh eyes, you need a subagent (or to invoke the skill from a subagent, which Claude Code now supports). The difference matters most for review and evaluation work, where the agent's prior context creates bias.

A skill is not magic. A bad SKILL.md is just a bad prompt with extra steps. Wrong description, the skill never loads. Vague instructions, the model follows them vaguely. The same principles that make a prompt work make a skill work.

How to actually use them

The shortest possible playbook.

Step one: spot the pattern. You know you need a skill when you have explained the same thing more than twice in different sessions and the model would have done it right if it had remembered. Or when CLAUDE.md is starting to grow a "how to do X" section that reads less like a fact and more like a recipe.

Step two: write the SKILL.md. Make the directory. Put the frontmatter at the top. The hardest part is the description. It has to read like a sentence the user might say. "Use when the user wants to publish a post to Gloss" is better than "Gloss blog skill." Specific verbs, named tools, the actual situation. The character limit forces the discipline.

The body should tell the model the steps. Not why. Not background. Steps. Where to look, what to read, what to run, what to write, what to check. Long reference material goes in separate files in the skill folder, loaded only if the model needs them.

Step three: test the discovery. Start a fresh session. Type the kind of thing the user would actually type. Watch whether the skill loads.

If it does not, your description is wrong. If it loads but the model does the wrong thing, your body is wrong. Both are cheap to fix.

A small clean rule. If you cannot show another person the description and have them guess correctly what the skill does, the description is not specific enough.

Six rules I keep coming back to

These are the things I tell people when they show me a skill that is not working.

One. The description is the skill. If the description does not match what the user actually says, the skill is invisible. Rewrite the description first, the body second.

Two. Facts go in CLAUDE.md, procedures go in skills. If a new session would benefit for every task, CLAUDE.md. If a new session would benefit only when running a particular workflow, skill.

Three. Skills are paid for in tokens once loaded. Keep the body tight. Move detailed reference material to separate files in the skill folder.

Four. A skill cannot make an agent safer. It can only encode a procedure. If you want safety, you want sandboxing, allowlisted tools, careful permission scopes, and human approval for destructive actions.

Five. Installing a skill from a stranger is closer to running a script than reading a doc. Open the folder. Read the SKILL.md and any scripts.

Six. A skill that no longer fits the way you work should be deleted. The point of skills is to make a workflow reliable, not to have a collection.

The shape this gives a real project

The version I run, after about a year of trying every combination, is small.

CLAUDE.md tells the model who I am writing for, what voice I write in, what I never use, and where things live. About a page. Loads once.

A handful of skills cover the workflows I actually have. One for publishing to Gloss. One for newsletter issues. One for trifectas. One for screenshots. One in progress for KDP. Each one is the steps and the conventions, nothing else. Each one loads only when needed.

A few subagents do the work that needs fresh eyes. The Humanizer and deep-detect run as separate passes on a draft and return a clean rewrite without seeing the rest of the conversation. A small worktree-isolated agent runs the KDP build so it does not pollute the main session.

Three layers, three jobs, one job per layer. Skills are the middle layer, the layer of procedures, the layer that has to be loaded on demand because there are many of them. A skill is a recipe Claude can pull off the shelf when the situation matches. It is not a security feature, a notes file, or a coworker, and it only earns its keep when you write the description well enough that it shows up at the right moment.

If you take one thing away from this, take that one. The description is the skill. Everything else is downstream.

What is in your skills folder right now that should probably be in CLAUDE.md, or in a subagent? Hit reply, I want to see.
